items.stem: Which best describes what Synnduit is?

options.text: A one-time data import / migration tool you run once
A long-running data synchronization engine that keeps a source and destination in sync over time
A reporting dashboard for viewing data

items.explanation: Synnduit is a continuous sync engine — it runs repeatedly and keeps source and destination aligned, rather than copying once.

misconceptions.a: Confuses a one-time import with ongoing synchronization — the defining trait is that it runs continuously.
misconceptions.c: The Synnduit Dashboard sits on top of Synnduit to visualize history; it is not Synnduit itself.
misconceptions.d: Synnduit moves and reconciles data between systems; it is not a backup tool.

items.stem: Synnduit's tagline is "ETL meets version control." Explain what each half contributes, in one or two sentences.
rubric: ETL half: it moves/transforms data from a source to a destination
Version-control half: it tracks changes (down to the field) AND/OR remembers the source↔destination link so records are updated, not duplicated
items.sampleAnswer: Like ETL, it extracts data from a source and loads it into a destination. Like version control, it logs every field-level change and remembers which destination record each source record maps to, so re-runs update rather than duplicate.

items.stem: A teammate wrote a nightly script that copies all 5,000 staff from HR into the destination. After a week, the destination has tens of thousands of staff rows. Why does this happen, and what does Synnduit do differently?
rubric: Identifies the cause: the script has no memory of what it already created, so each run re-inserts everything (duplicates)
Contrasts Synnduit: it remembers the source↔destination link (mapping), so a later run updates the existing record instead of inserting a new one
items.sampleAnswer: The script keeps no record of what it inserted before, so every night it creates all 5,000 again — duplicates pile up. Synnduit stores a mapping linking each source staff ID to the destination record it created, so the next run finds that link and updates the existing record instead of duplicating it.

items.stem: What does the "version control" half of "ETL meets version control" refer to?

options.text: Synnduit stores its own source code in Git
Synnduit tracks every change down to the individual field and remembers source-to-destination links
You must use a specific version of .NET to run it
Each run overwrites the previous run's data completely

items.explanation: The phrase describes a behavior of the synced data: field-level change history plus remembered mappings — version-control-like qualities applied to integration.

misconceptions.a: It is about the data being synced, not Synnduit's own codebase.
misconceptions.c: This confuses a runtime requirement with the product's behavior.
misconceptions.d: Overwriting everything each run is exactly the ETL-only behavior Synnduit improves on.

items.stem: Which statements about Synnduit are true? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It runs repeatedly over the long term, not once
It tracks change history at the field level
It is open source (Apache 2.0) and built in .NET
It deletes and re-loads the entire destination on every run

items.explanation: Synnduit is a long-running, open-source .NET engine with field-level change history. It processes only changes (the delta) — it does not wipe and reload.

misconceptions.d: Full reload each run is the ETL-only model; Synnduit processes only the delta.
